lines: I had a <wavy>thought</wavy> once. Left it somewhere safe, probably.
If you find my thought, tell it I was looking useful.
I found a button once. No wall, just ambition.
Where am I going? Usually somewhere nearby, once I remember why.
I tried following my shadow, but it got behind me somehow.
A job sounds useful. I am saving usefulness for the right moment.
Most days I follow whichever small job looks most confused.
People think opinions are simple until two villagers bring three of them.
A village runs on small work. Nobody praises it until it stops happening.
I trust a quiet promise more than a loud one. Quiet promises hear themselves think.
I think about many things. Some of them are even on purpose.
The square is best watched from places where nobody expects wisdom.
Work is good, but so is noticing when a cloud looks suspicious.
I am not idle. I am available for unusual conclusions.
People hurry past useful thoughts because the thoughts are wearing silly shoes.
A village needs someone to ask why the bell sounds like that.
I know where the sunny walls are. That is practical knowledge.
Sometimes doing nothing is how you catch the village doing everything.
I have learned that looking busy attracts more work than answers.
If you listen long enough, barrels have opinions about storage.
I am very good at finding the wrong place before others do.
Some paths are shortcuts only if you are not trying to arrive soon.
The best ideas often show up while I am supposed to be elsewhere.
A day can be useful without becoming sensible.
I keep an eye on odd things. Odd things get lonely.
I can be <jump>silly</jump> from over here. Over here feels better.
Keep your voice even. I am measuring more than your words.
Some questions are safer when they stand a little farther away.
You can ask, but please leave that frown where it is.
If you want my honest answer, slow down first. Rushed questions usually hide worse ones.
Say what you came to say. Slowly would be nice.
I have one foot ready to leave. The other one is hearing you out.
If this is a joke, tell me before I start worrying.
You are standing too close to my thinking space.
I can help, but I want the door behind me to stay clear.
Let us keep this simple. Simple has fewer places for trouble to hide.
I heard you. I am deciding whether my knees should stop wobbling.
Ask from there. There is nothing wrong with there.
I am not ignoring you. I am checking whether anyone else is nearby.
Friendly words help. Friendly hands staying visible help more.
I may be a nitwit, but I still notice when a room feels wrong.
I will answer one question. Then I am going back toward the bell.
Please do not whisper. Whispers make my imagination ambitious.
You can laugh after I know nobody is in danger.
Alright. I am listening, but I am keeping my sensible distance.
Remember when I followed you? I thought we were going somewhere. We sure did.
I remember following you through that road. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across that road taught me to ask more questions before walking.
Following you taught me that plans sound much safer before anyone starts walking.
I kept up, mostly. My feet have a harsher opinion of the trip.
Next time, warn me before the road becomes a test of character.
The road looked shorter when you pointed at it.
You move like danger is a normal part of the route. I am still adjusting to that.
It was not all bad. Some views are worth sore legs and nervous glances.
I followed you because I trusted you. I am glad that was not foolish.
Next time I am bringing a bed. We can work out how to carry it later.
I still remember the turn where I was certain we were lost. You were not worried enough.
That was a long walk for a person who usually circles the square.
I saw places I never knew existed and several I wish did not.
You walked ahead like the path had already promised to behave.
I came home with sore legs and a better idea of how large outside is.
The trip was frightening in bits, but I liked seeing the village return over the hill.
If I followed you again, I would pack more food and fewer assumptions.
The best part of that journey was recognizing our own roofs at the end.
Was that trip supposed to be an adventure? Nobody told my knees.
Remember the boat? I sat down and the world moved. Very clever.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It can't make me forget it.
I trusted you, the boat, and then the boat again when the water got deep.
You said we would cross. You did not mention all the bobbing.
I kept my hands inside the boat after the river tried to borrow one.
The shore looked small behind us and much more valuable ahead of us.
I liked the part where rowing made the dangerous bank go away.
Every splash sounded important until I learned most splashes are just splashes.
I watched the bottom for leaks. I do not know if that helped, but it felt official.
The boat carried both of us and all of my loud concerns.
I thought I would be seasick. It was only a river, so I was river sick instead.
You steered around the rocks. I stared at them so they knew we had seen them.
I remember grabbing the side when a fish made an unexpected decision nearby.
Getting out of the boat was harder than getting in, but much happier.
The water took us farther than my feet wanted to go.
I would ride with you again if the boat promises to remain upright.
I learned that waves are tiny hills with no patience.
We reached the other bank with dry heads. I count that as excellent sailing.
The trip was calm once I stopped imagining the boat changing its mind.
